translation: In diseases of internal injury and the like, the qi of the heart and lung is already severed externally; one is of necessity lethargic and loves recumbence, heavy and indolent, unable to gather the four limbs. This is heat wounding the Original Qi. The spleen governs the four limbs, and since [the four limbs] are already seized by heat, there is no qi to move. The Classic states: "Heat wounds the qi," and again: "Heat then the bones melt and the sinews slacken." This refers to this. In external contraction of wind-cold, the qi of the kidney and liver is already severed internally. The kidney governs the bones [and] cold; the liver governs the sinews [and] wind. Since ancient times the diseases of the kidney and liver have been treated together, because they sustain each other in turn. Hence the Classic says: "The gallbladder governs the sinews; the bladder governs the bones." Whether suffering wind stroke or cold damage, on the day of contracting the disease one takes to bed and pillow; unless supported, one cannot rise; the sinews and bones become painful and cannot be moved or swayed. This is injury to the concrete substance. The Classic states: "Cold wounds the form," and again: "Cold then the sinews contract and the bones ache." This refers to this.
